lead: A Bezier curve is a smooth curve shaped by a small set of control points. The curve does not usually pass through the inner points; it is pulled toward them by blending functions. This gives designers an easy handle: move a point, and the curve bends. Bezier curves are used in font outlines, car body panels, animation paths and vector drawing software. The same idea extends to a Bezier surface, where a grid of control points shapes a smooth patch.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for how curves become polygon edges, and Unit 2 for affine transforms of control points.

blocks.text: Take n+1 control points P<sub>0</sub> to P<sub>n</sub> in the plane or in space. The degree n Bezier curve is a weighted sum of these points. The weight of P<sub>i</sub> at parameter t is the Bernstein polynomial. At t = 0 only P<sub>0</sub> has weight 1, and at t = 1 only P<sub>n</sub> has weight 1, so the curve always starts at P<sub>0</sub> and ends at P<sub>n</sub>.
B(t) = Σ<sub>i=0</sub><sup>n</sup> P<sub>i</sub> C(n,i) t<sup>i</sup> (1−t)<sup>n−i</sup>, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1
blocks.where: B(t) is the point on the curve at t; P<sub>i</sub> is control point i; C(n,i) is the binomial coefficient n!/(i!(n−i)!); t is the parameter.

blocks.text: For n = 3 the binomial coefficients are C(3,0) = 1, C(3,1) = 3, C(3,2) = 3, C(3,3) = 1. These are the 1, 3, 3, 1 coefficients of a cubic. A cubic Bezier is therefore a weighted average of four points. The inner control points P<sub>1</sub> and P<sub>2</sub> pull the curve, but the curve normally does not pass through them.

blocks.where: t is the curve parameter; P<sub>0</sub> to P<sub>3</sub> are the four control points.

blocks.text: De Casteljau's algorithm evaluates a Bezier point by repeated linear interpolation. Start with the control polygon P<sub>0</sub> to P<sub>n</sub>. For each neighbouring pair, take the point a fraction t along the segment. This makes n new points. Repeat on the new list until one point remains. That last point is B(t). When t = 0.5, every step is a midpoint.

items: List the n+1 control points P<sub>0</sub>, P<sub>1</sub>, ..., P<sub>n</sub>.
For each adjacent pair, form P<sub>i</sub><sup>(1)</sup> = (1−t)P<sub>i</sub> + tP<sub>i+1</sub>. The superscript (1) is the level number, not an exponent.
Replace the old list with the new list and repeat until one point remains.
The final point is B(t). At t = 0.5 each step is just a midpoint.

blocks.text: The figure shows a cubic at t = 0.5. P<sub>0</sub> to P<sub>3</sub> give Q<sub>0</sub>, Q<sub>1</sub>, Q<sub>2</sub>; these give R<sub>0</sub>, R<sub>1</sub>; these give S<sub>0</sub> = (2, 1.5), a point on the curve.
A Bezier curve has a fixed set of useful properties.

items: It interpolates its end points: B(0) = P<sub>0</sub> and B(1) = P<sub>n</sub>.

The tangent at t = 0 is along P<sub>1</sub> − P<sub>0</sub>; the tangent at t = 1 is along P<sub>n</sub> − P<sub>n−1</sub>. For a cubic the derivatives are 3(P<sub>1</sub> − P<sub>0</sub>) and 3(P<sub>3</sub> − P<sub>2</sub>).
The curve lies inside the convex hull of its control points.
Affine invariance: apply a translation, rotation, scaling or shear to all control points, and the transformed curve is the same as transforming every curve point.
No local control: moving one control point changes the whole curve except the end points that are not moved, because every Bernstein weight is nonzero for 0 < t < 1.

blocks.text: A Bezier surface is the tensor product of two Bezier curves. A grid of control points, called a control net, replaces the control polygon.
B(u,v) = Σ<sub>i=0</sub><sup>m</sup> Σ<sub>j=0</sub><sup>n</sup> P<sub>i,j</sub> C(m,i) u<sup>i</sup>(1−u)<sup>m−i</sup> C(n,j) v<sup>j</sup>(1−v)<sup>n−j</sup>
blocks.where: P<sub>i,j</sub> is a control point in the net; u and v run from 0 to 1; m and n are the degrees in the two directions.

blocks.text: Two Bezier curves join smoothly. C<sup>0</sup> continuity needs the last point of the first curve to equal the first point of the second. For two cubics with P<sub>3</sub> = Q<sub>0</sub>, C<sup>1</sup> continuity needs Q<sub>1</sub> − Q<sub>0</sub> = P<sub>3</sub> − P<sub>2</sub>, so the tangent vectors match. If only the tangent direction matches, that is weaker geometric continuity, not C<sup>1</sup>.

figure.caption: De Casteljau at t = 0.5: halving the legs of P0 (0,0), P1 (1,2), P2 (3,2), P3 (4,0) gives Q0, Q1, Q2, then R0 and R1, then S0 = (2, 1.5), which is on the curve. The Bernstein sum (P0 + 3P1 + 3P2 + P3) ÷ 8 lands on the same point.

spec.aria: A cubic Bézier curve with its dashed control polygon P0 (0,0), P1 (1,2), P2 (3,2), P3 (4,0), the first-level midpoints Q0, Q1, Q2 joined, the second-level R0 and R1 joined, and the final point S0 (2, 1.5) on the curve.

examples.question: A cubic Bezier curve has control points P0 = (0, 0), P1 = (1, 2), P2 = (3, 2), P3 = (4, 0). Find the curve point at t = 0.5 using the Bernstein form. Verify it by de Casteljau. Give the tangent vectors at t = 0 and t = 1.
steps: Degree n = 3. The coefficients are C(3,0) = 1, C(3,1) = 3, C(3,2) = 3, C(3,3) = 1. At t = 0.5 the weights are 1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8.
examples.answer: The point is (2, 1.5); tangents are (3, 6) at t = 0 and (3, −6) at t = 1.

traps: Assuming the curve passes through every control point. A Bezier curve interpolates only its two end points. A repeated end point (P<sub>0</sub> = P<sub>1</sub>) only makes the start tangent zero; it does not create a new interpolation point, and repeating an inner point does not make the curve pass through it.
Using degree n equal to the number of control points. With n+1 points, the degree is n, which is one less than the point count.
Dropping the 1, 3, 3, 1 coefficients in the cubic case. They come from the binomial coefficients and are not optional.
Forgetting the factor n in the derivative. The tangent at t = 0 is n(P1 − P0), not just P1 − P0.
Confusing a Bezier control polygon with a Bezier surface control net. The net is a grid for a tensor-product surface.

quiz.q: Write the Bernstein form of a degree n Bezier curve.
quiz.a: B(t) = Σ<sub>i=0</sub><sup>n</sup> P<sub>i</sub> C(n,i) t<sup>i</sup>(1−t)<sup>n−i</sup>, with P<sub>i</sub> the control points and 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

quiz.q: Why does a Bezier curve lie inside the convex hull of its control points?
quiz.a: Each point B(t) is a weighted average of the control points. The Bernstein weights are nonnegative and sum to 1, so B(t) is a convex combination of the control points.

quiz.q: For a cubic Bezier with P0 = (0, 0), P1 = (0, 1), P2 = (1, 1), P3 = (1, 0), find B(0.5).
A designer moves one inner control point of a cubic Bezier. Explain which part of the curve changes and why this differs from a B-spline.
quiz.a: Moving an inner control point changes the whole interior of the Bezier curve, because the Bernstein weight of that point is nonzero for every t between 0 and 1. A B-spline has short-range basis functions, so only a small piece changes.

quiz.q: State C0 and C1 conditions for joining two cubic Bezier curves with first P0..P3 and second Q0..Q3.
quiz.a: C0: P3 = Q0. C1: the derivatives match, so 3(P3 − P2) = 3(Q1 − Q0), giving Q1 − Q0 = P3 − P2.

quiz.q: Why is de Casteljau's algorithm numerically stable?
quiz.a: Every step is a convex combination of two points already in the convex hull. The values stay inside the hull, with no large cancellation or growth, so evaluation is stable.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Bezier curves lead into NURBS, which add weights so circles and conics can be exact; CAD kernels use them for trimmed surfaces. Font engines flatten Beziers into short lines before rasterising. Search terms: de Casteljau algorithm, Bernstein polynomial, NURBS, tensor-product surface.
